title: The Arabian Oryx Comes Back
summary: How the Arabian oryx survives in the desert, why it vanished from the wild, and how zoos, reserves, and rangers brought it back.
poll: People can fix the harm they have done to wild animals.

versions.title: The Oryx Is Back
versions.text:
Look at that white animal. It is an oryx. It has two long horns. They are thin and straight.

The oryx lives in the desert. The sun is hot there. Its white coat helps it stay cool. It can go a long time with no drink. It gets water from the plants it eats. Rain may fall far off. The oryx can tell. It walks there. It finds new grass.

Oryx live in a herd. A herd is a group. When it is hot, they rest in the shade.

Long ago, hunters shot too many. By 1972, none were left in the wild.

But a few lived in zoos. Staff kept them safe. They had young. The herd grew.

Then some went back home. Oman set a herd free in 1982. Saudi Arabia did it in 1990. Now they live in a big reserve. Men with trucks keep them safe.

Now more than one thousand live in the wild. The oryx is back!

Look at that white animal on the sand. It is an Arabian oryx. It has two long horns. They are thin and straight, and they can be as long as your arm.

The oryx lives in the desert. The sun there is very hot. Its white coat helps it stay cool. The oryx can go for weeks with no drink. It gets water from the plants it eats. It also licks dew in the cool night. It can tell where rain has fallen far away. Then it walks there to find fresh grass.

Oryx live in a herd. In the hot part of the day, the herd rests in the shade of a tree.

Long ago, hunters with guns and cars shot too many. By 1972, no oryx were left in the wild.

But a few still lived in zoos. People kept them safe, and they had babies. Slowly, the herd grew.

Then some went back home. Oman set a herd free in 1982. Saudi Arabia did the same in 1990. The oryx now live in a big reserve. Rangers guard them.

Today, more than one thousand live in the wild. The oryx came back!

versions.title: The Arabian Oryx Comes Back
versions.text:
Imagine a white antelope standing motionless on the red sand of the Arabian desert. It has two long horns that are slender, straight, and sharply pointed. This is the Arabian oryx, and its horns can grow longer than a child's arm. When the animal is viewed from the side, the two horns sometimes appear to merge into a single one, which may explain old legends about creatures with one horn.

The oryx is extraordinarily adapted to survival in the scorching desert. Its white coat reflects sunlight, which keeps the animal considerably cooler than a darker coat would. An oryx can survive for weeks without drinking, because it obtains most of its moisture from the vegetation it eats and from dew that collects on leaves overnight. It can also apparently detect where rain has fallen at a great distance, and it will travel for many hours to reach the fresh grass that sprouts afterward.

Oryx live together in a herd. During the hottest hours, they rest in the shade of trees in order to conserve energy and water.

Unfortunately, hunters equipped with rifles and fast vehicles killed far too many of them. By 1972, the oryx was officially extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number of oryx still survived in zoos. In captivity, people protected the animals and helped them breed, so the herd gradually expanded.

Eventually, some oryx were returned to their desert homeland. Oman released a herd in 1982, and Saudi Arabia followed in 1990. Rangers now guard them inside enormous protected reserves.

The oryx was once critically endangered, but today more than one thousand live in the wild, which makes its return a remarkable success story.

versions.title: The Return of the Arabian Oryx
versions.text:
Imagine a white antelope standing motionless on the red sand of the Arabian desert, its two long horns rising slender, straight, and sharply pointed above its head. This is the Arabian oryx, whose horns can grow longer than a child's arm. When the animal is observed from the side, the two horns sometimes appear to merge into a single one, which may help to explain ancient legends about creatures with one horn.

The oryx is extraordinarily well suited to its harsh desert habitat. Its pale coat reflects intense sunlight, keeping the animal considerably cooler than a darker coat would, while its broad hooves help it walk across soft sand. An oryx can survive for weeks without drinking, because it obtains most of its moisture from the vegetation it eats and from dew that collects on leaves overnight. It can apparently also detect rainfall at a great distance, and it will travel for many hours to reach the fresh grass that sprouts afterward. Oryx live in herds, and during the hottest hours they rest in the shade of trees to conserve energy and water.

Tragically, hunters equipped with rifles and fast vehicles killed far too many of them, and by 1972 the oryx was officially extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number still survived in zoos, where people carefully protected them and helped them breed, so the captive population gradually expanded.

Scientists then decided to reintroduce oryx to their desert homeland. Oman released a herd in 1982, and Saudi Arabia followed in 1990. Rangers now guard the animals inside enormous protected reserves.

In Saudi Arabia, the animals were released into Mahazat as-Sayd, a fenced reserve northeast of Taif, and later into Uruq Bani Ma'arid, at the edge of the Empty Quarter. Rangers track the herds, sometimes with radio collars, and watch for poachers. The work has not always been easy, because in Oman illegal hunters captured many oryx during the late 1990s, and the population there shrank dramatically. That setback reminded everyone that protection must continue.

In 2011, a global conservation organization changed the oryx's status from endangered to vulnerable. It was the first animal that had vanished from the wild to recover so far, and today more than one thousand roam freely again.

versions.text:
Imagine a white antelope standing motionless on the red sand of the Arabian desert, its two long horns rising slender, straight, and sharply pointed above its head. This is the Arabian oryx, whose horns can grow considerably longer than a child's arm. When the animal is observed in profile, the two horns sometimes appear to merge into a single one, which may partially explain ancient legends about mysterious creatures with one horn.

The oryx is extraordinarily well suited to its harsh desert habitat. Its pale coat reflects intense sunlight, keeping the animal considerably cooler than a darker coat would, while its broad hooves allow it to travel efficiently across soft sand. An oryx can survive for weeks without drinking, because it obtains most of its moisture from the vegetation it consumes and from dew that accumulates on leaves overnight. It can apparently also detect rainfall at a remarkable distance, and it will journey for many hours to reach the fresh grass that sprouts afterward. Oryx live in herds, and during the hottest hours they rest in the shade of trees to conserve both energy and water.

Tragically, hunters equipped with rifles and motor vehicles killed far too many of them, and by 1972 the oryx was officially extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number still survived in zoos, where people carefully protected them and encouraged them to breed, so the captive population gradually expanded.

Scientists subsequently decided to reintroduce oryx to their desert homeland. Oman released a herd in 1982, and Saudi Arabia followed in 1990. Rangers now guard the animals inside enormous protected reserves.

In Saudi Arabia, the animals were released into Mahazat as-Sayd, a fenced reserve northeast of Taif, and later into Uruq Bani Ma'arid, on the western edge of the Empty Quarter. Rangers monitor the herds, sometimes by fitting individuals with radio collars, and patrol constantly for poachers. The work has not always progressed smoothly, because in Oman illegal hunters captured many oryx during the late 1990s, and the population there shrank dramatically. That setback demonstrated that protection must continue long after animals are released.

In 2011, an international conservation organization changed the oryx's official status from endangered to vulnerable. It was the first animal that had completely vanished from the wild to recover to that extent, and today more than one thousand roam freely once again.

versions.title: The Return of the Arabian Oryx
versions.text:
Imagine a white antelope standing motionless on the red sand of the Arabian desert, its two long horns rising slender, straight, and sharply pointed above its head. This is the Arabian oryx, whose horns can grow considerably longer than a child's arm. When the animal is observed in profile, the two horns occasionally appear to merge into a single one, which may partially explain ancient legends about mysterious creatures possessing a solitary horn.

The oryx is extraordinarily well adapted to its unforgiving desert habitat. Its pale coat reflects intense sunlight, keeping the animal considerably cooler than a darker covering would, while its broad hooves enable it to travel efficiently across shifting sand. An oryx can survive for weeks without drinking, because it obtains most of its moisture from the vegetation it consumes and from dew that accumulates on leaves overnight. It can apparently also detect rainfall at a remarkable distance, and it will journey for many hours to reach the fresh vegetation that sprouts afterward. Oryx live in herds, and during the hottest hours they shelter beneath trees to conserve both energy and precious water.

Tragically, hunters equipped with rifles and motorized vehicles slaughtered far too many of them, and by 1972 the oryx was officially extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number still survived in zoological collections, where specialists carefully protected them and encouraged them to breed, so the captive population gradually expanded.

Scientists subsequently decided to reintroduce oryx to their ancestral desert homeland. Oman released a herd in 1982, and Saudi Arabia followed in 1990. Rangers now patrol the enormous protected reserves where the animals live.

In Saudi Arabia, the animals were released into Mahazat as-Sayd, an extensive fenced reserve northeast of Taif, and subsequently into Uruq Bani Ma'arid, on the western edge of the Empty Quarter. Rangers monitor the herds continuously, sometimes by fitting individuals with radio collars, and they patrol constantly for poachers. The undertaking has not always progressed smoothly, because in Oman illegal hunters captured numerous oryx during the late 1990s, and the population there declined dramatically. That discouraging setback demonstrated that vigilant protection must continue long after animals are released.

In 2011, an international conservation organization officially changed the oryx's status from endangered to vulnerable. It was the first animal that had completely disappeared from the wild to recover to that extent, and today more than one thousand individuals roam freely once again.

versions.title: The Return of the Arabian Oryx
versions.text:
Imagine a white antelope standing motionless on the red sand of the Arabian desert, its two elongated horns rising slender, straight, and sharply pointed above its head. This is the Arabian oryx, whose horns can grow considerably longer than a child's arm. When the animal is observed in profile, the two horns occasionally appear to merge into a single one, which may partially explain ancient legends about mysterious creatures possessing a solitary horn.

The oryx is extraordinarily well adapted to its unforgiving desert habitat. Its pale coat reflects intense sunlight, keeping the animal considerably cooler than a darker covering would, while its broad hooves enable it to travel efficiently across shifting sand. An oryx can survive for weeks without drinking, because it obtains most of its moisture from the vegetation it consumes and from dew that accumulates on leaves overnight. It can apparently also detect rainfall at a remarkable distance, and it will journey for many hours to reach the fresh vegetation that subsequently sprouts. Oryx congregate in herds, and during the hottest hours they shelter beneath trees to conserve both their energy and their precious water.

Tragically, hunters equipped with rifles and motorized vehicles slaughtered far too many of these animals, and by 1972 the oryx was officially extinct in the wild.

Fortunately, a small number still survived in zoological collections, where specialists carefully protected them and encouraged them to breed, so the captive population gradually expanded over the following decades.

Scientists subsequently decided to reintroduce oryx to their ancestral desert homeland, so Oman released a herd in 1982, Saudi Arabia followed in 1990, and rangers now systematically patrol the enormous protected reserves where the animals live.

In Saudi Arabia, the animals were released into Mahazat as-Sayd, an extensive fenced reserve northeast of Taif, and subsequently into Uruq Bani Ma'arid, a protected area on the western edge of the Empty Quarter. Rangers monitor the herds continuously, occasionally by fitting individuals with radio collars that transmit their locations, and they patrol constantly to deter poachers. The undertaking has not always progressed smoothly, because in Oman illegal hunters captured numerous oryx during the late 1990s, and the population there declined dramatically within a few years. That discouraging setback demonstrated that vigilant, well-funded protection must continue long after captive animals are released into the wilderness.

In 2011, an international conservation organization officially reclassified the oryx from endangered to vulnerable. It was the first animal that had completely disappeared from the wild to recover to that extent, and today more than one thousand individuals roam freely once again across the Arabian Peninsula.

wrong.A: Mahazat as-Sayd is northeast of Taif, and neither reserve is inside the city.
wrong.B: The article does not place this reserve in Oman.
wrong.D: The article does not mention a zoo in Riyadh.

questions.stem: What happened to the oryx's status in 2011?
options: It was listed as extinct in the wild.
It changed from endangered to vulnerable.
It was moved from vulnerable to endangered.
It was removed from every list because it was safe.
questions.why: The article says a conservation organization changed the status from endangered to vulnerable in 2011, a sign of recovery.

wrong.A: The oryx was extinct in the wild in 1972, not 2011.
wrong.D: Vulnerable still means at risk, so it was not removed from the lists.

questions.stem: Scientists decided to reintroduce oryx to their desert homeland. What does reintroduce mean?
options: To study an animal closely in a laboratory
To bring an animal back to where it once lived
To move an animal into a zoo for good
To count how many animals live in an area
questions.why: The prefix re- means again. The oryx had lived in the desert before, and scientists brought it back there.

wrong.A: The oryx was released into the desert, not kept in a lab.
wrong.C: Reintroduction moved oryx out of zoos, not into them.
wrong.D: Counting animals is a survey, not a reintroduction.

questions.stem: What lesson does the setback in Oman most strongly suggest?
options: Oryx cannot survive in Oman's hot, dry climate.
Released animals still need protection long afterward.
Radio collars frighten oryx away from the reserves.
Captive breeding should stop once a herd is released.
questions.why: Even after oryx were released, poachers captured many and the population fell sharply, showing that protection must continue.

wrong.A: The oryx declined because of illegal hunters, not the climate.
wrong.C: The article does not say collars frighten oryx.
wrong.D: Nothing in the article suggests stopping captive breeding.

questions.stem: Why do rangers most likely fit some oryx with radio collars?
options: To keep the animals warm on cold desert nights
To help the oryx find water
To track the herds so rangers can protect them
To make the oryx easier for visitors to photograph
questions.why: The collars send signals, so rangers can follow the herds across huge reserves and notice problems such as poachers.

wrong.B: The oryx finds water from plants and dew on its own.
wrong.D: The article links rangers to protection, not photography.

questions.stem: Why does the author point out that the oryx was the first animal that had vanished from the wild to recover to vulnerable?
options: To show how unusual and important its recovery was
To argue that other animals are not worth saving
To explain how oryx get water in the desert
To describe what the oryx looks like
questions.why: Calling it the first such recovery emphasizes that the oryx project was a rare, historic conservation success.

wrong.B: The author never suggests other animals should not be saved.
wrong.C: Water is explained earlier and is unrelated to this point.
wrong.D: Its appearance is described at the start of the article, not here.

questions.stem: How does the oryx's situation today compare with its situation in 1972?
options: It is still extinct in the wild, but more live in zoos.
It is now safe everywhere and needs no rangers.
Its numbers are about the same, but it lives in different places.
It was gone from the wild; now over a thousand live wild.
questions.why: In 1972 the oryx was extinct in the wild, while today more than one thousand roam freely and its status is vulnerable.

wrong.A: The oryx is no longer extinct in the wild.
wrong.B: The article says rangers still patrol, and the oryx is still vulnerable.
wrong.C: Its wild population rose from zero to more than one thousand.

HIGH.prompt: Was the Arabian oryx project a complete success? Use evidence from the article to explain your answer.
checklist: I stated a clear opinion about the project.
I used evidence such as the 2011 status change and the setback in Oman.
I used at least two key words, such as reintroduce or population.
